title: Multi-Region & Disaster Recovery
subtitle: Watch an entire region fail, and see how much data and time each recovery design costs you.
learn: What RPO and RTO mean and how they drive design and cost
Why replicas are not backups, and what each one protects against
Active-passive versus active-active regions and their trade-offs
How data residency rules limit where data may be copied
Why untested failover plans tend to fail, and how drills fix that

steps.title: A whole region goes dark
steps.body: Your shop runs in region A, a cluster of data centers in one metro area. Today a power and network failure takes the whole region offline: every server, including the database. Multi-region design is the plan for that day, by keeping a second copy of the system in another region. Two questions decide the plan. How much recent data can you afford to lose? And how long can you afford to be down?
steps.idea: Disaster recovery starts with two business questions, not with technology.
steps.caption: All traffic flows to region A today.

steps.title: RPO and RTO
steps.body: RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data you can lose, measured as time. An RPO of 5 minutes means the newest 5 minutes of writes may vanish. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long the service may stay down, including the time to notice and decide, not just to repair. The business picks both targets. Tighter targets cost more, so a payments ledger and a recommendations cache should not share the same numbers.
steps.idea: RPO is data lost, RTO is time lost. Pushing either toward zero gets steeply more expensive.
steps.caption: Two clocks start ticking when the region fails.

steps.title: A standby copy in region B
steps.body: Region B keeps a replica (a live copy) of the database. Writes commit in region A, then stream to B asynchronously as the write-ahead log (WAL), the ordered list of changes. We do not wait for B to confirm each write, because that would add roughly 60 to 150 ms to every write. The cost is replication lag, the delay before B catches up. It is typically under a second, but can spike under load. Anything not yet shipped when A dies is lost, so lag is your real RPO.
steps.idea: Asynchronous replication is fast, but its lag is exactly the data you can lose.
steps.caption: Writes stream to B about one second behind.

steps.title: A replica is not a backup
steps.body: A replica copies every change, including your mistakes. If a bad deploy runs DELETE without a WHERE clause, the replica faithfully deletes the same rows a moment later. A backup is a separate point-in-time copy, kept with logs so you can restore to just before the mistake. Replicas guard against hardware loss. Backups guard against human error, corruption and ransomware. Keep at least one copy immutable or in a separate account, and remember a big restore can take hours.
steps.idea: Replicas give availability. Backups give history. You need both.
steps.caption: The bad write replicates, but the vault keeps history.

steps.title: Region A fails
steps.body: Now region A is unreachable. The router's health checks fail and requests to A time out; noticing takes about a minute here. The replica in B holds everything up to about one second ago, so roughly that much data is stranded in A. The danger: if you promote B while A is only cut off, not dead, both sides might accept writes (split-brain). Teams prevent this by fencing the old primary (blocking it from accepting writes), and often by requiring a human to confirm.
steps.idea: The failure is easy to see. Deciding that it is real is the hard part.
steps.caption: Region A stops answering; B has a copy.

steps.title: Active-passive failover
steps.body: In active-passive, B is a warm standby: running at reduced size and ready to scale up. An engineer promotes the replica to primary, scales up the app servers and flips the router so users go to B, as the animation shows. With a rehearsed runbook (the written step-by-step recovery plan) this commonly takes 5 to 30 minutes. A cold standby, not running until needed, takes hours. A pilot light keeps only the data tier running. The outcome here: RPO of about 1 second and RTO of about 10 minutes.
steps.idea: Active-passive is cheaper and simpler, but you pay in minutes of downtime and an idle region.
steps.caption: Traffic shifts to B after the replica is promoted.

steps.title: Active-active
steps.body: In active-active, both regions serve users all the time. Losing one just means the router sends everyone to the other. That one must already have spare room: each region is sized to carry the full load alone, so each runs at 50% or less normally. RTO is seconds to about a minute, depending on how fast the router notices and clients stop using cached answers. With asynchronous replication RPO is still about the lag. The price is write conflicts, where two regions change the same record at once, so you need conflict rules or a home region per user.
steps.idea: Active-active buys near-zero RTO at the cost of conflict handling, double capacity and complexity.
steps.caption: Both regions serve traffic and sync.

steps.title: Data residency
steps.body: Laws such as the GDPR limit moving personal data outside the European Economic Area unless safeguards apply, and some countries require data to stay in-country. Suppose EU data lives in region A and region B is outside the EEA, so B may not hold a copy. Recovery then uses backups in another region inside the same jurisdiction. Assume logs are archived every 5 minutes and a restore takes about 90 minutes. Both RPO (up to 5 minutes) and RTO (90 minutes) are far worse than with a live replica.
steps.idea: Where recovery data may live is a legal limit. Check it before choosing the failover region.
steps.caption: EU data may not be copied to B; recovery uses backups in another EU region.

steps.title: Failover drills
steps.body: A plan nobody has run is a guess. Real failures expose stale credentials, too little capacity in region B, DNS caches that ignore your short TTL (how long resolvers may keep an answer), and runbooks that depend on a tool living in the dead region. Teams run drills: first shift a small share of traffic, then a full game day that really fails over, and measure the actual RPO and RTO against the targets. Practise failing back too, and restore from the vault into region B to time that path.
steps.idea: Only a measured drill tells you your real RTO. Practice turns a guess into a number.
steps.caption: A drill shifts traffic to B and measures the clock.

steps.title: Pick the cheapest design that meets the targets
steps.body: Set RPO and RTO for each system from the cost of downtime and data loss. Use replicas for fast failover and backups for history, because they solve different problems. Active-passive is simpler and slower. Active-active is faster and harder. Check data residency before copying data anywhere, and drill regularly so the numbers on paper are the numbers you really get.
steps.idea: Replicas for speed, backups for history, drills for truth.
steps.caption: Targets, copies, and drills together form the plan.

quiz.q: A team's database replica lags the primary by about 2 seconds under normal load. The region fails and they promote the replica. Roughly what is their data loss?
options: None, because the replica has a full copy
About 24 hours, the backup interval
About 2 seconds of recent writes
Only writes from the failed region's cache
quiz.why: Asynchronous replicas trail the primary by the lag, so writes in that window never left the failed region. Lag is effectively your RPO.

quiz.q: A buggy migration deletes a customer table at 14:02. Why does the cross-region replica not save you?
options: Replication copies the delete to the replica within moments
Replicas only store indexes, not rows
Replicas are read-only so they cannot be restored
Cross-region replication is too slow to matter
quiz.why: Replication is faithful, including mistakes. You need point-in-time backups with logs to restore to 14:01.

quiz.q: The business says the service may be down at most 30 seconds in a region loss. Which design fits best?
options: Nightly backups copied to another region
A cold standby rebuilt from infrastructure code
Active-passive with a manual runbook
Active-active with enough spare capacity in each region
quiz.why: Only a design where the other region is already serving traffic reaches RTO in seconds. Manual promotion typically takes minutes or more.

quiz.q: You add active-active writes in two regions. What new problem must you solve that active-passive avoided?
options: Reads can no longer be served locally
Two regions may update the same record concurrently, creating conflicts
DNS can no longer route users
Data can no longer be backed up cross-region
quiz.why: With a single writer there is one order of changes. With two writers you need conflict rules, home-region ownership, or a globally consistent store.

quiz.q: A runbook has never been executed. What is the most likely outcome in a real region failure?
options: It works, since the steps are written down
It works, but only if the replica is promoted first
Actual recovery takes longer than the stated RTO because of hidden gaps
It succeeds, since region B has been idle and is therefore up to date
quiz.why: Untested plans hide expired credentials, capacity shortfalls, and dependencies on the failed region. Drills reveal them before they cost you.

cheatsheet.def: Recovery point objective: the most data, measured in time, you accept losing. Set by lag or backup interval.
Recovery time objective: the longest acceptable outage from failure until service is restored.
Replicas copy changes live for fast failover, mistakes included. Backups are separate point-in-time history for restoring.
One region serves traffic; another stands by. Simpler and cheaper, RTO in minutes to hours.
Several regions serve traffic at once. RTO in seconds to a minute, but needs spare capacity and conflict handling.
Two regions both believe they are primary and accept conflicting writes. Prevent with fencing (blocking the old primary from accepting writes), often combined with quorum or human confirmation.
Legal rules limiting where data and its copies may be stored. It constrains replica and backup placement.
A planned drill that fails over for real and measures actual RPO and RTO against targets.
